title: "Missing outcomes in public health surveillance and surveys"

**To the BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026**

## Project objective

I want to understand who is represented when a public health outcome is missing. I will use two course datasets to study missing hospitalization information in waterborne outbreak reports and missing systolic blood pressure readings in a national health survey. Each dataset will have its own analysis vignette on the project site.

## Vignette 1. Hospitalization reporting in waterborne outbreaks

**Research question.** Among U.S. waterborne outbreaks reported to CDC from 2009 through 2023, how does the availability of hospitalization information differ across drinking water, treated recreational water, and untreated recreational water?

I will use `waterborne` from the course `finalproject` package, an extract of the CDC National Outbreak Reporting System. The unit of analysis is one reported outbreak. I will keep records whose primary transmission mode is water and use `water_exposure` to assign them to the three groups. I will report how many records have mixed, other, or undetermined exposures before excluding them from the main comparison. [CDC data and field definitions](https://data.cdc.gov/Foodborne-Waterborne-and-Related-Diseases/NORS/5xkq-dg7x/about_data)

The binary outcome is whether `info_on_hospitalizations` reports a positive count of people with known hospitalization status. A blank or zero count means the report provides no usable count of people with known status. An outbreak with known status can still record zero hospitalizations. For each exposure group, I will report the number of outbreaks, the median number of illnesses, and the percentage with hospitalization information. I will also standardize the percentages to the same distribution of outbreak onset years because reporting practices and the mix of water exposures may change over time. If severe cases are more likely to have their hospitalization status recorded, the available records may overrepresent severe illness.

## Vignette 2. Missing systolic blood pressure in NHANES

**Research question.** Among adults aged 20 and older with a positive NHANES examination weight in 2009–2012, how does the percentage with a missing systolic blood pressure reading vary by age group?

I will use `NHANESraw` from the NHANES R package, which includes data from the 2009–2010 and 2011–2012 survey cycles and retains the survey design variables. The unit of analysis is one participant. I will group age as 20–39, 40–59, and 60 or older and report how many records lack age or a usable examination weight. The binary outcome is whether the combined systolic blood pressure measure (`BPSysAve`) is missing. For each age group, I will report the participant count, the survey-weighted percentage missing, and the distribution of available readings in mm Hg. I will check whether the age pattern holds across sex and survey cycle, since measurement completion may vary by participant characteristics or cycle. [NHANES package documentation](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/NHANES/refman/NHANES.html)

As a secondary analysis, I will check whether accounting for missing readings changes the estimated mean systolic blood pressure. I will combine examination weights across both survey cycles using CDC guidance and estimate the survey-weighted mean among adults with a reading. I will then reweight the available readings to match the age, sex, and survey-cycle distribution of all eligible adults and report the difference between the estimates in mm Hg. This adjustment assumes that within each of these groups, adults with and without a reading have similar mean blood pressure. [CDC survey weighting guidance](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/tutorials/weighting.aspx)

## Planned reporting

The pkgdown site will contain both vignettes, with reproducible R functions for repeated summaries, tables and plots of missingness, and a discussion of the findings and limitations for each dataset.
